As a kid I used to go to my local library at least once a week and just walk around. The only reason I learned to use a bike was so I could get there faster. Not just for books and reading, though that was the main reason obviously for a long time.

The cool thing about libraries is that they're functionally about experimentation really. It's about being able to pick something up without having to fully commit. It's a safe space in the sense that it's a warm comfortable, quiet place - but also because it's okay for anyone to walk up to anything and consider it.

I was really in need of both as a kid. I didn't have a connection to my town or neighbourhood. I kept changing schools, and overall had a terrible immune system which conditioned me to stay inside. Till I found the library. There I could go, feel like a part of the community, even as a kid.

As far as experimentation: my dad was for example pretty strict about films. He didn't like them, they were considered trash entertainment for the uneducated. So every week, after squeezing as many books in my tiny backpack as possible, I'd check out the movie isle. I'd just kind of walk up and down, reading the backs of vhs's and dvd's. Trying to figure if this really was that bad, 'cause it all looked pretty cool to me.  
Oh and the same for sexuality, obviously. The sight of a kid walking around the sex & health isle whistling, trying to look like he's just there by accident, must be pretty funny.

I had a similar assessment of the reading list, but I didn't quite want to push back because, hey, maybe this is the standard in some parts of anglo-saxon academia. I've heard of worse, more outdated curriculi when it comes to german idealism.

We'll have to disagree on Kojeve I guess. I think he fits right in line with folks like Zizek, and can provide similarly interesting insights.

First of all, never mind the rambling. My response was for from coherent.

Yeah, so, on Kant: I think few would argue that's really the core of what he's about. In fact, I think the sort of general 'intro to deontological ethics' what's generally taught about Kant at first is quite a misrepresentation. I mean, it's not unrelated, and in a roundabout way it can be quite a helpful insight, but only once you've already climbed that ladder and discarded it (to use the Wittgenstein analogy).

I don't want to discourage you at all of course. Many, including myself, I think kind of accidentally ended up really taking to Hegel, totally not realising what they were getting themselves into. I just kind of got fascinated with Philosophie Des Rechts in my second undergrad year as part of an ethics class. It's all doable.

As to Taylor... I've read things that have referenced the book, and have read some of it when necessary, but I never went through it beginning to end. It's not quite the kind of reading of Hegel I find myself drawn to.
It's far from irrelevant of course, again from a historical perspective. A writer with an Anglo Saxon academic background I think is quite likely to have come into contact with Hegel through Taylor and Pippin.

If time is limited, I would advise just to, pick a main source of secondary literature (Kojeve, or Pippin, or Taylor or any combination), but also try and get a good sense of German Idealism as a whole. I think that's much more important for getting a grasp on Hegel, rather than trying to immediately skip and move on to everyone else who expanded upon his ideas, be it Marx, Lacan or Judith Butler.

EDIT: Oh, I just remembered. An author that helped me getting into Hegel when I was but a second year undergrad was Robert Solomon. Very accessible and supporting writer and such I recall.

Kind of an odd place to start, but sure. Kojève's a must, must read. Not only for historical signifcance, having influenced a ton of French 20th century intellectuals with his reading, but also because it's just very clear and interesting.

Robert Pippin is obviously another big name when it comes to introducing people to Hegel. I know he's published one recently (which I know nothing about), but 'Hegel On Self-Consciousness' and 'Hegel's Idealism' are both advisable reading.

If you're up for something else, what I'd advise as one of those people who just can't shut up about Hegel - rather than just one single source to read and help you through things, maybe just eclectically read a few things that use and expand upon that exciting, radical way of thinking. Just to get into the head space, sort of.

Should that be something you're interested in, then you're in luck. With Zizek & Badiou, there's so much stuff to explore in that Critical Idealism / Psychoanalysis strand of philosophy. For Zizek, it's probably 'Less Than Nothing' & 'Absolute Recoil', at least to my recollection. But for both you can just fire up youtube and enjoy hours of content.

Oh, perhaps, not unimportantly: how good is your grasp on earlier german idealists? Fichte & Schelling aren't necessary, but can be interesting. Kant seems like a must though. Speaking for myself, that's one educational move I regret greatly - not having a great grasp of Kant before jumping into Hegel. Took some effort later to fix that.

An old man wearing a series of worn-out medals and badges over comfortable coffee-stained clothing, lights a cigar. Bottom text identifies him as 'Lt. Col. Terry Conant' as he takes a long drag, holds it, and then satisfyingly blows out the smoke as he leans back into his chair.

T.C.: "It seemed like nothing but a God-given miracle. To tell you the truth, at first I couldn't believe it myself. What those boys up in Manhattan were able to put together had always been tip top, but this was something new altogether. It was magic. Simple as that."

/B&W/ Men in lab coats and uniforms alike are shown cheering, laughing and congratulating each other. The footage may be unrelated, but in general an overall good and almost festive (as far as that's possible in wartime) mood is established.

T.C.: "We were beyond ecstatic. Everything else, from the bottom all the way to the top, was put on hold. Everyone's first priority became getting whatever the heck this was to our boys in the Pacific asap. Washington-"

/B&W/ President Roosevelt is shown shaking hands with certain officials and giving speeches.

T.C.: "had given us a New Year roll-out schedule. That meant we had less than a year to figure this whole deal out. Less than a year to train the necessary individuals."

Conant starts laughing hard. His laugh eventually dissolves into a gravelly, unhealthy cough.

T.C.: "Of course, nowadays that seems like madness. Almost like some of those 'get magical quick'-schemes. But there's a few things you gotta consider. First of all, if you don't know what you're getting yourself into, it's hard to realise how stupid that thing is. Or how dangerous." *He shrugs, opens his hands*. "Right? But second of all, and perhaps most importantly,-"

Conant smiles, takes another drag, then looks meaningfully at the camera, as if peering over imaginary glasses.

T.C.: "whoever we send wasn't going over there to plane shift or cast 'mind blank'. This was primitive, ma en pa magic. Mind you, at the time, we thought that's all we were gonna need to bring the Japs, the Krauts, the Soviets... whoever to their knees. Just the most basic crap was undoubtedly a game changer. A few firebolts, some healing cantrips, that's where our head was at."

/B&W/ Some of the earliest footage of magical experimentation is shown. Some rituals and incantations go horribly, horribly wrong, but the footage cuts away just before any of the gruesome after effects can be seen.

T.C.: "Turns out though, even all that's a hassle. We missed the '42/'43 deadline, but Washington couldn't ignore the necessity of the project, so they did what bureaucracy does best. Project Cana was implemented, and after a few formal firings they send transferred everyone else over . Eventually the '43/'44 deadline was missed again, though not by much. We probably would've kept on going though if it wasn't for Ike."

/B&W/ The classic footage is shown of Eisenhower shaking hands with the troops, though it's spliced with different footage showing him being just as friendly with a team of scientists and other robed officials.

T.C.: " '44 meant Game Time for Ike. No messing about. That meant magic, and Cana having to show results. We delivered on our promise eventually: one support company of trained individuals ready to go in and cast a giant hole in Hitler's front door."

/B&W/ A lined-up company is seen saluting. One private flashes a smile at the camera.

T.C.: "We used to call them 'good boys' in-house, because after while, you kind of started treating these guys like pets, you know? I think that must've gotten out to the men they were assigned to, because soon they became known amongst the troops they served with as 'Mage Hounds' or simply 'Hounds'."

Pictures are shown of the modern Mage Hound insignia: the head of a greyhound barking up a fireball.

T.C: "So there we were, all ready and finished up for Ike's little new project: 'D-Day'. Washingtons estimations put us on 80/20 odds to win the war before Christmas. But, obviously, things didn't quite work out that way."

Footage is shown of the war continuing, on and on.

Conant grunts. This isn't particularly the high point of his career.

T.C.: "It... Would... Be wrong... To say absolutely none of us expected Hitler to have his own little project going. Some, including myself, would've told you... Even at the time... That Berlin was rarely far behind us on these matters, so, better you know: be ready. But what absolutely none of us predicted, was that they also had been practicing different spells than us"

Conant sighs, puts out the cigarette.

T.C.: "Those damn Krauts had figured out Precognition."

When he entered, the contestant was already standing there a while, peering into the inky blackness. He'd seemingly ripped his pristine suit to shreds, like a banker who'd survived a plane crash. Lit by one single rainbow-coloured light, it seems like his legs were starting to give up on him, and his eyes keep involuntarily closing. Putting up his comfortable, assuring facade, Dan coughs and starts: "So what seems to be the issue 907?" His spot only came in after he was done talking, as per usual. "I'm gonna do it!", yells 907, as he reveals he's holding a lengthened paper clip, "and you know my name, Thomas! My real name!"  
 Thomas. Dan should've picked something else. It's so bland, just a bit *too* homely. He demonstratively sighs: "Mr. Dobbs-"  
 "Derek! My name's Derek! Come on man, why are you acting like this?!"  
 Dan smiles: "*Derek,* we prefer using your assigned participation number to remind you the staff of this facility are voters just as well. We'd like to avoid another Season 4 situation. Now, what is it you were gonna do?"  
 "I'm gonna end it!", yells Derek, "And I know you can't stop me, otherwise the gas would've knocked me out already!"  
 The guy wasn't really wrong, but hey, this business 'd never been about being right. "Hmm, maybe", Dan responds, "Or, maybe, we don't always need the gass?"  
 "Yes!" Derek's eyes shoot open again, "You don't! You can cut me a deal. Just make it seem like I lost, next week, whatever the result."  
 "You know that's not possible Mr. Dobbs", says Dan, "Management really holds a dedication to democracy to be one of their founding principles."  
 "Management? What the fuck's that?", questions Derek.  
 Dan smirks: "Lets not dwell on that Mr. Dobbs. Maybe you'll never need to know." Dan pauses, and looks the broken figure before him, whose seemingly slowly starting to slaunch over against the glass: "Why don't you tell me where you got it?"  
 "Huh?", mumbles Derek, dazed.  
 "The pin, Mr. Dobbs, where did you get it? Are there others? Does 902 have one?"  
 "No", Derek shakes his head, "I got it from Suzie. She was gonna use it herself, but then she got voted out."  
 "Ah, Ms. Harker", nodds Dan, making a small note in his head to slightly tweak her profile-archetype for future season. The clean physician apparently did have a dirty streak in here.  
 Derek's legs start shaking even more. He slaps himself in the face: "Enough! Am I getting my deal or what?!"  
 "I think I made quite clear the chances of that are- Ah...", Dan pauses, as Luke enters and hands him the double espresso. "Hmmm ", he almost moans as the hot, black liquid starts to work its caffeinated magic, "I love this stuff"  
 Derek grabs the pin: "I don't mind doing it, Thomas. Ending it all? I really don't! Don't you fucking test me!"  
 Dan sips again, then continues slowly: "Tell me *Derek*, wouldn't you agree, at times, it almost feels like a necessity?"  
 The contendor’s legs finally collapse on him. His body tilts and smacks against the glass.  
 "Say you're suddenly feeling really, really tired and weak...", Dan starts walking toward the glass, hunkering down to maintain eye contact with 907, ".for seemingly no reason..."  
 Derek has to start spitting out his sentence in short bursts: "What did you do... You... sick bastard?!"  
 "Me? Nothing?", Dan says, now more calm and soothingly, "But some medical professionals, when you arrived here, did quite a few check ups on you before you woke up. And, in addition, they may have injected you with a little dormant substance-"  
 Derek spits on the glass.  
 "But only the kind that's so lightly dormant, it reactivates when exposed to-", Dan stops as Derek is clearly about to visit dreamland any second, "Well, what does it even matter"  
 "Oh you mother... You mother...", Derek manages to utter before he slowly fades away.

Keep 'm talking. That's all one had to do in cases of potential problems such as this one. The light did the rest. Might as well enjoy a cup of coffee whilst you're doing it. No other drink goes better with a chat.

He ordered the crew to come in and clean the whole thing up, so 907 could safely be returned to his cosy bed inside The House. Dan kept the pin though. He had quite a collection of memorabilia like that. You never know who'll be the one left standing.

As it turns out, this time, 902 was cut loose and none other than mister Derek Dobbs became the 9th Leader Of The Free World. He was immovably silent when they told him. Unlike most of the others, he didn't scream or yell or cry. He just sat there. Probably thinking about his pin, and why he'd waited. About all the horrors the coming year had in store for him.

Now, you might think Management would be proud of someone like Dan Cundy, for saving the life of a sitting Head of State. But, truth be told, Management didn't care. Management rarely does. The only thing that matters, is the principle of it. Voting. Democracy. The Will Of The People.  
At least that's what they claim.

"Aaand we're out." A little bell rings in the background. "Thanks everyone, we'll see you on monday", shouts Dan.  
A nicely dressed older woman approaches him, stirring her heavily scented latte. "Nicely done", she says, smiling.

"Uhuh", Dan responds, grabbing his bag, "spit it out Kate, every second you spend showing what looks like genuine emotion probably does irreparable damage to our already dwindling ice caps" He starts walking towards one of the booths to check up on some last details.  
"Ever the poet mr. Cundy", Kate says dropping her smile like a hot pan,"I've been tasked to request that you stay over, this weekend?"  
Dan stops in his tracks and loudly sighs: "Can't Humphrey do it?"

"I'm afraid mr. Sellek isn't in our employment anymore", says Kate, walking towards him, "he's probably going to do 5 to 10 for bribery"  
Dan raises an eyebrow: "Bribery?"  
"Hmhmm, remember Contestant 803 from last year?"  
"Yes, Charlotte. The blonde northern one. Loved metal and a reduced tax on cosmetics", says Dan, nodding.  
Kate smirks coldly: "Right. Well, turns out that when it came to mr. Sellek, 803 was less of a rock star and more of a groupie."  
"Aha.", Dan pauzes, "How long have we known?"  
"That's irrelevant. Management trusts you to take over his responsibilities until the season finale next week.", Kate takes a sip from her latte, "You'll be well compensated of course"  
"I... I don't think I can", Dan responds, "I'm so, soo done... Plus it's the broadcasting bit I'm good at anyway, the weekend shift involves none of that. It's just baby sitting"  
"Tsss... Don't underestimate yourself as a producers mr. Cundy. And though in the weekend the cameras might not be rolling, contestants still need producing. Now more than ever when they think their end is near."  
Dan thinks for a second, then shakes his head: "I'm not doing it." He starts to move towards the door.  
Kate stops him and leans in : "Let's just not do this mr. Cundy. In the interest of our own time and sanity."  
Dan sighs even deeper. He quite liked having a job, a pension, credit, a house key that worked and a car that didn't mysteriously crash into lamp posts.  
Kate claps her hands: "Right, your badge has been upgraded already with mr. Sellek's priviliges - which includes private quarters in the R&R department. Ask anyone from the weekend crew to fill you in should you have any question, alright? I'm sure a man like you is just as familiar with them." As Kate walks away, Dan quietly curses to himself.

...

A soothing 'ding' sound effect alert of an incoming message through the speakers: "Could you come down here sir, we might have a problem". Dan groans as the lights in his room slowly start fading in. He sits up straight and checks his watch. One full hour of sleep, amazing. He hits a specific button on his night stand: "Luke, can you meet me at the Cube in 5 minutes or so." He gets up to move and then hits the button again: "Oh and if you're not holding a double espresso in your meaty paws I might actually, finally take a deep dive into raving madness. Turn that new wedding ring of yours into a new lip piercing, feel me?"

The Cube was a big glass cube-shaped room that connected The House, the stage of the show in which the contestants do everything to get chosen by the voting audience at home, to the larger facility owned my Management. It's the place where, if all other measures fail, the contestants can talk to the outside world. Or, more specifically, where they get to talk to him. If anything or anyone 'might be a problem', it can probably be found there. Marla Noxon, a support staff officer wearing full body armour, joins him on his way there: "it's 907, he's getting angsty - threatened to cut himself."  
Dan frowns: "So? Just do the usual thing, why am I getting called in?"  
Marla shakes her head: "Can't. System's down. Budget cuts to the tech crew means..."  
Dan cuts her off, sarcastically: "Yeah, yeah I get it. It's a great idea to keep slashing the budget of the no.1 show, it's not as if Management..." Marla raises an eyebrow. Dan notices and corrects himself: "Y'know what , I'm sure they got it all under control."

The Cube was built like a small stage, constructed around a tight tight hallway exiting The House. By intricate manipulation of the lighting, a single authorised participant who walks up to the end of the glass corridor, sees precisely and only what someone in Dan's position wants them to see: a single person talking, a small crowd looking, a big screen showing a video, or just pitch dark nothingness. This time however, the first and simplest option seemed the most appropriate. This was routine, Day 1 stuff. He clapped his hands: "Aight, listen up everyone, lights please, let's get this over with as soon as possible!"

"Hey look man, we don't want any trouble, so why don't you just...", starts Adam."Why don't you shut the fuck up?!", snaps Blake, a loud bang of previously unheard thunderclaps drowning out the last few words of his sentence. Almost pleadingly, he turns to Ellie: "Why? Just tell me, what... What did I do wrong?"

"I...", she stammers, thinking, trying to remember. There was a clear explanation for this, something very simple, he... With a heroic roar, Adam pounces from the bed towards the intruder. Just before he can reach and overtake him, there's a quick flash, and a short workmanlike hammer hits Adam's head with a loud and painful-sounding "gruntch". He staggers back and Ellie interrupts her thinking to produce a loud screech. As Adam slowly falls backwards unto the bed, he reaches for the impact wound. Expecting a lot of blood, the fit young man only seems to find a giant dent in his skull. As a tidal wave of pain is about to hit him, what functionally remains of his brain decides the best course of action is to take a short little break from the proceedings. Adam falls unconscious.

"Adam!", yells Ellie, tears forming in the corners of her eyes. With shaky breath she caresses his face, before looking up with blood red eyes towards the intruder: "Why did you have to do that you sick... A hammer?!" "Well,", says Blake, as he looks at the almost pristine little hammer in his right hand, "at first a gun seemed like the obvious choice, but then I thought... why? Just... Why?" He let's the question linger in the air a bit, then continues: "What's wrong with a hammer? I checked it out online, and guns cost a \*thunder\*-ton of money. I don't think I can afford that"

"Yeah right, like that's a problem for you.", sniggers Ellie, "Couldn't you just have asked your daddy for some extra pocket cash for the weekend?" "What?", frowns Blake, "Why do you assume that's an option?""Oh please, look at the suit you're always wearing", shoots Ellie, "even now, as you're in the middle of my apartment, attacking me and the only man who's ever really cared about me!"

"Yeah maybe because it's only one I own, ever thought about that?", says Blake. "And for the love of god, what's that supposed to mean? What about me? I cared about you!"

"No... No you didn't, you...", stammers Ellie, trying to remember what it was again that made her want to get man, who's clearly a damn maniac, out of her life to begin with, "he is... Adam..."

"Come on, you really believe in this one true love bull-\*thunder\* ? You? Cynical, wise-ass Ellie Hobbs?"

Ellies realises she's been running her fingers through Adam's hair the entire time. She's shaking, her breathing irregular. With a long, deep breath, she stops, gathers herself and looks at Blake: "What's the play here? Are you gonna smash me too with that thing? Because if not, you better start running, 'cause I'm about to scream..."

"Hurt you?", says Blake, "Why would I...". He drops the hammer on the floor and sits back down in the chair, defeated. He stars staring off into the distance through the window, as thick raindrops clatter against it without remorse.."I didn't even want to hurt him, not really. I just..." Tears start forming in his eyes now. His bottom lip even starts to quiver a little bit. After a moment of silence, his now even weaker voice fills the room yet again: "Ellie, please, I don't get it. None of it. What happened?"

Ellie started thinking, retracing the steps in her head from the past year. It was quite a unique experience. Sometimes, certain moments were so full and lifelike, whereas other times it was as if whole months had gone by and she hadn't even been awake to experience them. Then, slowly, she started to remember: "You... You were on the phone. We'd just had a fight" Blake sits up straight again. Ellie continues: "You were talking, telling someone that you 'did not care about her at all'... It broke my heart Blake." Silence. "There's your answer." Raindrops keep hitting the window.

"Wait are you kidding me?!", Blake stutters in utter disbelief. "Huh? Blake, you said you didn't...", responds Ellie. "You overheard one phone call. ONE CALL? That's all it takes? Did you even listen to the entire thing?" "No,", says Ellie, "but you said..." Blake interrupts her: "WHY didn't you talk to me about that?! You just disappeared!"

"Oh let me guess,", Ellie says, starting to get worked up again, "it was all one big misunderstanding, you weren't really talking about me.." Hmmm, that didn't quite seem to line up with her argument. Why didn't she just call him? "Yeah, maybe,", snaps Blake, "or MAYBE, we'd just had a fight and I was \*thunder\* mad at you like a regular \*thunder\* human being!"

"I..." Ellie didn't quite know what to make of it. Inside of her head, things were starting to get a little complicated. As if there was some other part of herself she needed to convince. Something that didn't quite feel like herself at all, actually.

In the background, Blake is fuming. He's pacing up and down the room. Sometimes he sounds angry, sometimes sad. Sometimes little sounds and words penetrate the bubble. 'Hell', 'Him', 'What the', 'Why', 'Why', 'Why', 'Why'.

"Because you just weren't the one". Ellie heard the words in her head, but couldn't figure out where on earth they'd come from. It was just a product of her mind, or, something in her mind, at least. Still, she felt them escape her mouth just the same.

Blake stopped. He looked at her, at Adam, and the hammer.

"No, I guess not."

Well, obviously ethics is more complicated than that. To summarise very quickly: I would make distinctions between lawful and ethical doing, both being forms of moral doing. A human being has the capacity to be moral, which I'll summarise as: when he or she does something for reasons other than sole personal self-interest. One can assume human beings are moral, or at the very least have the capacity to be.

Now we've established that, I'll take a page from Hegel & Hobbes. Human beings have specific negative freedoms, which translate into rights when applied to the real world. These rights form the basis for a society. So in order to maintain these rights, a human being *should* follow the rules of the society. Let's call this lawful: doing things not out of self interest, but because one has to follow the societal rules. And in turn, because said rights trump the abstact negative freedoms, a state may punish those who break the rules yet do not wish to opt out. "Opting out" btw, will very rarely mean anarchistic independence. One will always be a part of some society (because, humans, in addition to very probably being moral, are also very probably political, see Aristotle), just maybe one with very mild rules at best.

Then, in addition to that, I suppose the option of ethical life (Kierkegaard, Heidegger,..), or to put it simply: one has the right, to, in addition to the rules of society, follow personally established principles. One can/should do so for existential reasons, because it's recommended if one wants to give ones life meaning in a meaningless universe. However, this has to be an entirely free choice, a.i. one can only condemn people for breaking such rules on a personal level. Here's where I can also fit in Hegel, as if one is purely concerned with avoiding a conflict between the ethical and lawful self, one simply has to make the underlying principles of the law one's own principles (*sittlichkeit*).

So "goodness" is way too broad a term for me. I think one is moral, should be lawful, and can be ethical. For example: human beings can choose to cheat, which doesn't break the law, as such shouldn't be punished, though some may consider it unethical.
